1: Reported swallowing difficulties among US adults aged 18 years and older in 2022 and 2025. Points indicate survey-weighted prevalence standardized to the projected US 2000 adult age distribution; horizontal lines indicate 95% confidence intervals. Circles denote 2022 and squares denote 2025. Event counts and valid-response denominators are unweighted and therefore do not reproduce weighted percentages. Open markers identify estimates flagged for sparse contributing age cells or high relative standard error. The overall population and the separate stroke-history population are the central analyses; the no-stroke comparison is supporting. The overall group includes unknown stroke status and overlaps both stroke-history groups. Standardized estimates use a common reference age distribution, rather than the actual distribution of stroke survivors. Source: National Health Interview Survey public-use data
2: Absolute age-standardized prevalence differences between 2025 and 2022 by outcome and stroke history. Points indicate differences in percentage points; horizontal lines show 95% confidence intervals. The dashed zero line denotes no difference. Reported swallowing difficulty is the primary outcome. Substantial difficulty represents the response “a lot”; prolonged symptoms represent at least 180 days during the preceding year. Both secondary outcomes use population denominators, with valid primary-negative responses coded as negative and missing follow-up responses retained as missing. Open markers flag sparse contributing year-by-age cells or high relative standard error. Secondary outcomes and the no-stroke comparison are supporting analyses, with nominal intervals and no multiplicity adjustment. Source: National Health Interview Survey public-use data
3: Differences in reported swallowing difficulties between 2025 and 2022 across analysis methods, overall and separately among respondents with stroke history. Points and horizontal lines show prevalence differences in percentage points and 95% confidence intervals; the dashed line denotes no difference. Squares mark the principal direct age-standardized contrast. Crude estimates describe the observed weighted population. Direct standardization uses the projected US 2000 adult age distribution. Survey-weighted logistic models adjust for year, age group and sex, with marginal predictions averaged over the same age distribution and a fixed 50:50 male:female distribution. Separate models are fitted for the overall population and the stroke group. Restriction to confirmed self-responses excludes proxy and ambiguous response status using conservative year-specific classifications; these classifications are not fully equivalent across years and the restriction changes the target group. Direct estimates remain sensitive to sparse contributing age cells; model-based margins borrow information across age cells and remain subject to model assumptions. Source: National Health Interview Survey public-use data
4: Age-specific differences in reported swallowing difficulties between 2025 and 2022, overall and separately among respondents with stroke history. Points indicate survey-weighted prevalence differences in percentage points; horizontal lines show 95% confidence intervals. The dashed zero line denotes no difference. Age is age at interview, not age at stroke onset; the public-use age variable is top-coded at 85 years. Counts show unweighted events and valid-response denominators in each survey year. Open markers flag sparse contributing cells or high relative standard error. These age-specific comparisons support interpretation of the adult analyses and use nominal intervals without multiplicity adjustment. Source: National Health Interview Survey public-use data
S1: Sensitivity to interview period and missing responses. Points and horizontal lines indicate age-standardized prevalence differences between 2025 and 2022 in percentage points and 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line denotes no difference. Restriction to interview quarters 1–3 retains annual weights without recalibration. The two extreme scenarios assign all missing primary responses to yes in 2022 and no in 2025, or vice versa. Their intervals represent sampling uncertainty conditional on each assignment and do not form a confidence band across missing-data mechanisms. These scenarios do not address complete interview nonparticipation or unknown age and stroke status. Source: National Health Interview Survey public-use data
